verdict.content_summary: Marketing homepage for Cursor, a subscription AI coding agent platform (IDE + cloud service). Core offerings: agentic development where you hand off coding tasks, cloud agents that run autonomously in parallel on Cursor-hosted machines, an 'Automations' feature for always-on agents triggered by schedules or triggers, presence across terminal/Slack/GitHub, multi-model selection including Cursor's in-house Composer model, self-hosted machines (changelog), and heavy enterprise social proof (NVIDIA, Stripe, Fortune 500). It's a positioning page, not a technical document — mechanisms are described only at the feature-name level.

grabs.what: The 'Automations' pattern: always-on agents triggered by schedules or triggers to build, maintain, and fix things without a human prompt
grabs.why: The user already runs local agents for daily work but the profile implies prompt-initiated sessions. Recurring trigger-driven agents are implementable today on their Linux VPS with cron/systemd + their existing agent harness, converting one-off agent runs into standing maintenance jobs (vault hygiene, dependency bumps, doc backfills) that emit results into their ingest queue. Stealing the pattern costs nothing and requires no Cursor subscription.

grabs.what: The parallel agent run-queue with structured per-run report artifacts (files explored, duration, summary, follow-up prompt hook)
grabs.why: The demo UI models exactly what the user values: agent-native output. Each run produces an absorbable record — scope of exploration, time spent, outcome, and a 'follow up' affordance — rather than requiring the human to watch. This run-report shape is directly reusable as a documented JSON/markdown schema for the user's own local agents, making runs triageable in their Obsidian vault the same way they triage articles.

aspects: Always-on agents triggered by schedules or external triggers for recurring maintenance rather than prompt-initiated sessions
Parallel isolated agent execution with a status-tracked task queue (this week / this month, running states)
Per-run structured report artifact: files explored, duration, human-readable summary, follow-up affordance
Graduated autonomy control ('autonomy slider'): scoped targeted edits at one end, full autonomous runs at the other
Multi-model routing with an automatic 'Auto/Suggested' per-task model selection layer
Same agent surfaced in every existing context (terminal, chat, PR reviews) instead of demanding a new environment
Cloud-hosted agent sandboxes where agents get 'their own computer' to build, test, and demo end to end
adjacency_queries: scheduled autonomous AI agents for recurring file and data maintenance workflows
parallel batch task orchestration with human review queue and per-task summary reports
adjustable autonomy levels human-in-the-loop control systems outside of coding

finds.name: Trigger.dev
finds.what_it_is: Open-source durable background-job engine for Node/TypeScript that handles job queuing with retries, parallel execution with concurrency control, and execution tracing.
finds.different_angle: Treats the triaged content's status-tracked queue and schedule-trigger aspects as buildable infrastructure instead of product features: its durable pause-and-resume for human review is the primitive behind a graduated-autonomy gate, so you assemble the queue, run states, and per-run artifacts yourself in code on your own VPS rather than adopting someone's scheduler UI.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: You run Node tooling and a Linux VPS, build your own projects, and reject tools duplicating what you already run — this hands you the parallel-queue and trigger aspects as a self-hosted, agent-callable library with BYO-key all the way down, and the per-run trace/output maps directly to your structured JSON artifact preference.

finds.name: OpenHands
finds.what_it_is: Open-source (MIT) coding agent platform; this talk covers running hundreds to thousands of agent instances concurrently on large refactors.
finds.different_angle: Takes the parallel-isolated-execution aspect to fleet scale, but swaps the cloud-hosted 'own computer' sandbox for local Docker sandboxes on your own hardware, and replaces per-run status-board oversight with human input aggregated at PR boundaries — review routing, not review queues.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: It's MIT-licensed and self-hosted next to your existing local agents and git-everything workflow, so nothing stores data outside your control; and the talk's core pattern (one human steering a thousand agents via PRs instead of reviewing each run) is exactly the kind of aspect you steal even when you skip the tool.

finds.name: Claude Code (headless / scheduled mode)
finds.what_it_is: Anthropic's terminal-based coding agent, driven headlessly through terminal tooling, its SDK, and CI rather than as an interactive chat session.
finds.different_angle: Implements the 'always-on recurring maintenance' aspect as plain infrastructure — cron- or CI-triggered non-interactive runs on machines you own — instead of the original product's managed scheduler and cloud sandbox, turning scheduled agent work into scriptable, diffable terminal output.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: It satisfies your hard constraints: CLI-first, works with your own API key (no embedded markup), runs on your Linux VPS alongside your current local agents, and emits agent-callable files that slot into your markdown vault's ingest queue instead of demanding a new environment.

tavily.sludge_check: Discarded MindStudio, Manus, and Fountain City (walled-garden SaaS/managed services violating the BYO-key and data-control rules) and the Kimi/Medium explainers (generic multi-agent content with no product fit); the three remaining finds pass because each is open-source or CLI/BYO-key native and reframes one specific triaged aspect from an infrastructure, fleet-scale, or self-hosted angle rather than suggesting another hosted product.

finds.name: FlowGate
finds.what_it_is: An open-source typed document pipeline where AI agents must register proof-of-work artifacts (Requirement → Task → Task Report) through an authenticated API before any handoff counts as done.
finds.different_angle: Inverts the per-run report artifact: instead of a human-readable summary handed to you after an autonomous run, the structured artifact is the enforcement mechanism — an agent can't claim completion without passing a typed gate approved by you or another agent, which also hard-codes the autonomy slider as per-handoff approval points rather than a global setting.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Open source, small, agent-callable via a documented API with typed artifacts — exactly your JSON-schema, agent-native-output style; its approval inbox is also a concrete pattern for your stated bottleneck of triaging which agent runs deserve an hour of attention.

finds.name: Allma
finds.what_it_is: An open-source orchestration engine for durable, async AI+human workflows with human approvals, external-event waits, and agent guardrails.
finds.different_angle: Treats scheduled and trigger-fired agents as durable state machines rather than clean-session cron runs: executions survive week-long waits, pause on external events, and run agents inside explicit guardrails with evidence trails — autonomy as auditable workflow state instead of a session-level slider.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Open source and self-hostable, so it can run on your Linux VPS beside your local agents instead of a cloud sandbox; it adds the external-trigger and approval semantics to your agent stack without a walled garden, subscription, or data leaving your control.

finds.name: Rills (batch & task approvals)
finds.what_it_is: A human-review layer whose approval nodes come in structured shapes: approve/reject, multiple choice, free text, batch fanout into dozens of individual cards, and reviewer checklists.
finds.different_angle: Attacks the human side of parallel agent execution: rather than gating or orchestrating runs, it designs the triage surface itself — how one reviewer processes the outputs of dozens of parallel runs (fanout cards, checklists) without drowning.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Your stated bottleneck is triage, not discovery; even if you never adopt the platform, its approval-shape taxonomy is a stealable pattern for the review queue over your own agents' per-run reports, and the docs are readable without a login.

exa.sludge_check: I discarded Claude Code Routines (it is the triaged product itself, not adjacent), Warp/Hivra/V7 Go/Backend.AI (cloud SaaS schedulers that demand their platform and conflict with your local-first, BYO-key, no-data-outside-my-control rules), Orkes (overlaps Allma with a heavier commercial runtime), and the two academic autonomy papers (not products) — the three remaining finds are open-source or pattern-level, each tied to your artifact/JSON, self-host, and triage-bottleneck specifics.
